text: Qadam is a Telegram delivery platform for Almaty. We focus on individual senders first, then small shops. We plan a launch period with zero commission. Later, the platform may charge couriers two to three percent per completed order. The exact rate and launch duration remain open. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Customers and Current Evidence
Individual senders first. Flower and other small shops later.
Registration does not prove active supply. Pricing feedback and willingness to pay have not been tested.

The team reported about one hundred registered couriers to the instructor and demonstrated the product. Users tested functions and the order journey. Their requests included prices, a better map, card payment and UI/UX improvements. We do not claim a pricing study, paid orders or a measured active-courier count. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.
Business Model Selection
A two-sided marketplace: senders request delivery, couriers fulfill it.
Proposed liquidity gates: 90% of valid requests accepted within 10 minutes; 95% of accepted orders completed.

We select marketplace commission, also called a rake. Couriers are the future fee-paying side. A completed delivery creates the fee, and delivery GMV is its value metric. Subscription is a poor fit for occasional senders. A fixed usage fee would ignore differences in order value. We use a temporary zero-fee launch, not an assumed freemium conversion funnel. The liquidity gates are suggested operating targets, not achieved data. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.
How Money Moves
Proposed wallet model. Example fare: KZT 1,500 at a 2% commission.
Wallet top-ups are prepaid balances, not revenue. Commission arises only on completion. No fee for a cancelled order.

Wallet: KZT 1,000 becomes 970.

The customer pays the courier directly. The courier funds a platform balance in advance. After a completed delivery, Qadam deducts the commission from this balance. A one-thousand-tenge top-up would leave nine hundred and seventy after one thirty-tenge commission. The customer payment is not routed through Qadam. Card collection and wallet implementation are future work. Refund and cancellation rules must be defined before launch. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.
Three Proposed Service Tiers
Assignment pricing architecture. No monthly subscription.
Only the 0% then 2–3% direction has been discussed. Business features and the final rate require a cost and WTP test.

preview: Starter / Launch | Pro / Standard | Enterprise / Future

text: This matrix meets the three-tier requirement without introducing a subscription. Starter is the zero-commission launch. Pro is a proposed two-percent standard service. Enterprise is a possible business service at up to three percent, with custom integrations, advanced security, a dedicated SLA and custom contracting. These enterprise capabilities are future proposals. Their costs and actual courier willingness to pay must be evaluated separately. All fees would be paid by the courier from the platform balance. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.
Value-Based Pricing
Primary value metric: completed-delivery GMV, not user seats.
The delivery tariff itself is still undecided. Commission acceptance and wallet funding need a real courier test.
PRICE FOLLOWS ORDER VALUE

Per KZT 1,000 of
completed-delivery value
WHY NOT “COST + 20%”?

Server cost does not measure
courier willingness to pay.

Cost-plus can miss the value
of finding delivery orders.

Wallet top-ups add switching
effort and money tied up.

Our value metric is the value of completed deliveries. At two percent, a courier pays twenty tenge for each thousand tenge of delivery income. At three percent, the fee is thirty. We reject cost plus twenty percent because server costs alone do not measure courier willingness to pay or the value of new orders. Wallet prefunding creates an additional switching cost: the courier has to set aside money and learn a new process. A zero-fee trial can reduce this friction, but its length is undecided. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.

On a fifteen-hundred-tenge order, an assumed twenty-percent fee is three hundred tenge and a two-percent fee is thirty. The reduction is two hundred and seventy tenge, or ninety percent. text: The team gave a monthly server budget of eight thousand three hundred tenge and said the map is currently free. For illustration, assume a fifteen-hundred-tenge delivery and five tenge of platform service cost per completion. At two percent, contribution is twenty-five tenge, so three hundred and thirty-two completed deliveries cover only the server. At three percent, the result is two hundred and eight. At zero percent the pilot needs funding. Including the illustrative sixty-thousand-tenge monthly acquisition budget raises the two-percent threshold to two thousand seven hundred and thirty-two deliveries. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.
Customer Acquisition Cost
Model unit: one newly monetized courier. Costs cover acquisition on both marketplace sides.
All acquisition figures are assumptions. The ~100 existing registrations are not the denominator for CAC.
CAC = KZT 60,000 ÷ 20 new monetized couriers = KZT 3,000

Because the future fee comes from couriers, we measure CAC per newly monetized courier. Allocate the costs of recruiting couriers and attracting sender demand to the same commercial cohort. The illustrative monthly pool includes digital ads, channel commissions, loaded sales labor and initial onboarding. Sixty thousand tenge divided by twenty new couriers with a first commission-paying delivery equals a CAC of three thousand tenge. These are assumptions, not actual campaign results. The same denominator must never include free registrations. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported. Pricing, wallet and paid plans are not implemented commercial results.
LTV and CAC Payback
Illustrative base case after launch: 2% fee, 20 deliveries/courier/month and 5% monthly churn.
No paid cohort exists yet. Churn, order frequency and costs are unvalidated. Contribution excludes fixed server cost.
MONTHLY CONTRIBUTION
20 orders × (KZT 30 − KZT 5) = KZT 500

Expected lifetime = 1 ÷ 5% churn = 20 months
LTV = KZT 500 × 20 months = KZT 10,000
6 months
Payback: 3,000 ÷ 500

At twenty deliveries a month, each producing twenty-five tenge contribution, one courier generates five hundred tenge per month for Qadam. A five-percent constant monthly churn assumption gives an expected lifetime of twenty months. LTV is monthly contribution divided by churn, which equals ten thousand tenge. Divide this by the three-thousand-tenge CAC to get three point three three. Simple payback is CAC divided by monthly contribution, or six months. There is no expansion or discounting. A thirty-six-month capped LTV gives a lower ratio of two point eight one in the workbook. These formulas do not prove retention. Reference: Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million (21 September 2021), CAC payback section. https://www.bvp.com/atlas/scaling-to-100-million Accessed 12 November 2026. The 3x and sub-12-month cloud hurdles are used as planning references, not marketplace funding criteria.
VC Reference Hurdles and Scenarios
Planning targets: LTV/CAC ≥ 3× and CAC payback < 12 months.
Cloud benchmarks are reference hurdles, not proof of marketplace readiness. All cases below are hypothetical.
Conservative check: base LTV/CAC capped at 36 months = 2.81×.

We compare scenarios with common venture-efficiency hurdles. The base case passes uncapped LTV/CAC and simple payback. A downside with fewer deliveries, higher churn and fewer newly monetized couriers fails. A three-percent fee improves the arithmetic but may reduce courier acceptance; retention is held equal only to isolate the fee change. This is not a recommendation to raise the fee without testing. The thirty-six-month capped base ratio is two point eight one, below three, which shows the sensitivity to assumed lifetime. Reference: Bessemer Venture Partners, Scaling to $100 Million (21 September 2021), CAC payback section. https://www.bvp.com/atlas/scaling-to-100-million Accessed 12 November 2026. The 3x and sub-12-month cloud hurdles are used as planning references, not marketplace funding criteria.
Commercial Validation and Next Decisions
The business model is proposed. Payment and pricing decisions remain open.

Our next step is a small commercial test, not an unsupported growth forecast. Agree the sender tariff, the length of the zero-commission launch, and whether the standard fee should be two or three percent. Confirm wallet top-ups, refunds and the low-balance rule. Card payment is a user request and remains future work. Measure actual completed deliveries per active courier, acceptance time, collection cost, fully loaded CAC and retained cohorts. Only then can the team validate value-based pricing and update the financial model. Source: team answers, 12 November 2026. Approximate courier count is team-reported.
